title: Business (mis)Use Cases of Generative AI
extended_summary:
This paper examines potential harmful business misuse cases of generative AI rather than educational applications or learning outcomes. The authors ask how generative AI might be misused at scale in business contexts, and they use participatory design fictions to explore how AI experts judge the plausibility, seriousness, and preventability of such futures.

The study used three fictional scenarios focused on generative text, audio, and video misuse: automated derivative novel writing, fake video evidence affecting insurance claims, and fabricated audio evidence in criminal cases. These scenarios were discussed in co-creation interview sessions with six AI software engineers, who first imagined their own future misuse scenarios and then reacted to the researchers’ 2030 scenarios. The data consisted of interview discussions that were thematically reviewed by two members of the research team.

Participants were adult AI professionals from a single research organization (IBM Research), not students, teachers, or school stakeholders. The context was a research interview setting rather than a classroom or educational implementation. No literacy intervention, K-12 population, or generative AI instructional use was studied.

The main conclusions are that experts saw generative AI misuse futures as partly plausible but contested in seriousness, with recurring themes around ubiquity of fakes, quality degradation, ownership questions, new market structures, and an arms race between generation and detection. Participants suggested that technological safeguards, provenance tools, regulation, legislation, and public education might mitigate harms. The paper is best understood as a qualitative HCI and ethics exploration of future risks, not as direct evidence about K-12 literacy uses of generative AI.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a workshop position/qualitative design-fiction study about business misuse cases of generative AI, not a K-12 educational intervention study. It includes only six AI engineer participants, no student sample, no instructional implementation, and no educational outcome measurement.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides no direct evidence of impact on K-12 learners, literacy, or classroom outcomes. Any educational implications are speculative rather than empirically estimated.
